Eggs of the Longspine snipefish Macroramphosus scolopax hatch after an incubation period of approximately 6.5 days [ab = approximately 6.5 days] when incubated at a stable temperature of 16 °C [T = 16 °C], a duration that aligns with the rapid embryonic development typical of small pelagic teleosts. The newly emerged yolk-sac larvae are lecithotrophic, deriving all their nutritional requirements from a large endogenous yolk reserve. The wet weight at birth of these larvae is estimated to be approximately 0.00038 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00038 grams], a mass that reflects the substantial yolk investment per egg, as inferred from the reported egg diameter range of 865 to 985 micrometers. This initial body mass is exceptionally modest, even by the standards of small-bodied marine fishes, and the prolarvae remain in a non-feeding state until their yolk is fully resorbed. The duration of this yolk-dependent stage, combined with the small size at emergence, likely imposes a strong selective pressure for encountering suitable planktonic prey shortly after the onset of exogenous feeding, a critical transition that determines early survival rates.

At the specified thermal regime of 16 °C [T = 16 °C], the post-hatching developmental trajectory of this species proceeds through a distinct juvenile phase before reproductive competence is achieved. The standard length at puberty, marking the onset of gonadal maturation, has been recorded at 8.4 cm [Lp = 8.4 cm], which corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of approximately 3.1 grams [Wwp = approximately 3.1 grams]. This size threshold, representing a roughly eight-thousand-fold increase in somatic mass from the larval stage, is reached over an extended growth period. The age at first reproduction, or the time when a spawning adult is first capable of participating in a spawning event, is estimated to occur at 547 days after hatching [tR = 547 days after hatching] under these same thermal conditions at a temperature of 16 °C [T = 16 °C]. This relatively prolonged pre-reproductive phase, spanning nearly one and a half years, suggests a life-history strategy that prioritizes the accumulation of substantial somatic reserves before allocating resources toward gamete production, a pattern that may buffer against interannual variability in food availability in its temperate shelf habitat.

As individuals continue to grow beyond the pubertal milestone, they ultimately approach an asymptotic body size that defines their maximum physical dimensions. The ultimate standard length for the Longspine snipefish has been documented at 16.8 cm [Li = 16.8 cm], which translates into a corresponding ultimate wet weight of 27.2 grams [Wwi = 27.2 grams]. This final body mass, achieved after several years of sustained growth, represents a substantial increase from the mass at puberty and reflects the species' capacity for continuous indeterminate growth, a characteristic common among many teleost fishes. Morphometric data indicate that the relationship between length and weight follows a strongly allometric scaling, which is typical for fishes with an elongated, compressed body form. The maximum recorded lifespan for this species has been documented in field studies as 2190 days [am = 2190 days] when maintained at a consistent 16 °C [T = 16 °C], a duration that is moderately extended for a small teleost and may reflect the species' relatively stable shelf habitat and iteroparous reproductive strategy. This longevity, spanning over six years, classifies Macroramphosus scolopax as a moderately long-lived member of the syngnathiform lineage, a life history that is comparatively extended relative to many small, pelagic planktivores.

Reproductive output in this species has been characterized through examination of spawning adults and planktonic egg surveys. Female Longspine snipefish produce approximately 35 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 35 eggs per day] and are capable of sustaining this fecundity daily over the duration of the spawning season, which can last for several weeks. This high fecundity strategy is consistent with an r-selected life history pattern, where early life stages experience high and unpredictable mortality in the pelagic environment. The spawning events themselves involve external fertilisation, with both gametes released into the water column during broadcast spawning. The demographic consequences of this high reproductive output are partially offset by the small size of the pelagic eggs and the vulnerable larval stages, which face intense predation pressure from gelatinous zooplankton and juvenile fishes during the first weeks of exogenous feeding.

Comparative life-history analysis places Macroramphosus scolopax within a moderate pace-of-life continuum relative to other species in the family Centriscidae. The species exhibits a standard length at puberty of 8.4 cm [Lp = 8.4 cm], which is reached approximately 547 days after hatching [tR = approximately 547 days after hatching] under the 16 °C [T = 16 °C] thermal regime typical of its Mediterranean and eastern Atlantic habitats. This relatively late maturation, combined with a maximum lifespan of 2190 days [am = 2190 days], suggests a life-history strategy that buffers against environmental stochasticity through iteroparous reproduction across multiple spawning seasons at a temperature of 16 °C [T = 16 °C]. The ultimate wet weight of 27.2 grams [Wwi = 27.2 grams] also places the species near the upper end of the size spectrum for its genus, a trait that may confer advantages in terms of fecundity and competitive dominance within the zooplanktivore guild. Ecological observations indicate that these fish form large, demersal aggregations over sandy and muddy substrates during the daytime, dispersing at night to feed on zooplankton in the water column, a behavioral pattern that likely contributes to their relatively high reproductive and somatic growth rates.
